Slay the Spire is a very addicting game too say the least. One minute you’re buying it on sale for 6 bucks, (it’s worth full price regardless) the next thing you know, you’re pushing almost 200 hours of play time. It’s an easy to play game that’s peaceful and super easy to just pickup and play for an hour whether you’re sitting down at your PC or at the Doctors office using Steam link waiting for your appointment. Would I change anything? Maybe add more content like cards and relics, but realistically it’s a completed game and Slay the Spire 2 is out, I just want more ways to go infinite. If you play it you’ll know what that means. Regardless, it’s a 10/10 game that’s easy to play, get into, visually appealing, and addicting. You don’t need a ton of hours to beat it starting out with Iron Clad, but I’ve seen some people 100% the game in about 150 hours of play time. No run you do is exactly like the last. The game can run on a toaster too, I don’t have a toaster but for those to do, this is a safe game even for those on a laptop that’s 5 years old. There’s an RNG factor, but it just adds to it instead of hurting the experience of playing. So what are you waiting for? Slay the Spire!

review

[b]"Slay the Spire" is a solid indie deck‑building game that, despite being well executed, fails to stand out. It certainly offers a large pool of cards and characters with unique playstyles and abilities, allowing the player to experiment with different builds and tactical approaches. The difficulty curve is well balanced, giving players time to learn its mechanics before gradually becoming more challenging, while the various modes add a few extra hours of playtime. Yet, it never truly impressed me. First of all, it’s not really a roguelike (as advertised), and there’s almost no continuity between runs except for a few cards and items you unlock. There’s no effort to tell even the slightest story or include meaningful lore behind the characters and enemies. The visuals feel generic and the animations are too static. Most importantly, it doesn’t feel like it offers anything genuinely new or refreshing to the deck‑building genre. It’s solid and well built, but I honestly don’t understand the buzz around it. 


Manometer: 7/10[/b]


The good
- Well‑balanced gameplay with a fairly large deck of cards to choose from, giving the player the opportunity to try various builds — more defensive, more aggressive, or focused on each character’s special abilities. It has some strategic depth and requires thoughtful planning behind each build. 
- Each character has its own distinct playstyle with unique mechanics and abilities that make them feel different and add replayability. It’s interesting that even after finishing the game with one character, switching to another requires learning their strengths and weaknesses almost from scratch. 
- Although after a few hours you’ll probably have seen every enemy and they become repetitive, for a small indie game it offers a respectable variety of enemies and bosses. Many of them have unique abilities and attacks that require specific builds to defeat them without losing too much HP. 
- Good difficulty curve that offers the right amount of challenge. Early battles are easy enough for new players to understand the mechanics and build their decks, while later stages become increasingly demanding. It never feels unfair, and during most runs you’ll learn something new about the character's strengths and what’s necessary to beat the game. 
- Like most deck‑building games, luck is a core element. Sometimes it’s annoying when you don’t draw the cards you need, yet the game is designed well enough to make you want to open every chest and defeat every elite enemy to see what reward you’ll get. 
- It offers various modes — daily challenges, custom mode, Ascension mode — which can extend playtime for a few more hours. 
- Despite the music playing constantly in the background, it’s quite good and fits the gameplay, so it never becomes tiring. 

The bad
- It’s advertised as a roguelike, but it really isn’t. You gradually unlock some cards and relics for future runs, but that’s not enough. Unlocking a new weapon in a shooter doesn’t suddenly make it a roguelike. Characters don’t gain experience or become stronger through runs, and there are no new abilities acquired from previous attempts. Each run is completely separate from the last. There isn’t even a hint of continuity in the lore or enemy reactions (like “Do you remember me?”) to suggest that runs are connected somehow.
- It’s a small indie deck‑builder, sure, but there is absolutely no story and the lore is barely existent. Characters and bosses have no backstory at all. It’s unbelievable that they didn’t make even the slightest effort to give your journey some purpose. It feels like a mathematical puzzle with random visuals that say nothing. 
- Despite offering a good amount of deck‑building options with large card pools and variations in attacks, relics, and potions, it offers nothing truly new or refreshing. We’ve seen countless games using the same terms like weak, vulnerable, poisoned, etc. 
- Gameplay is well balanced and luck always plays a role in these games, but I felt that each character has two or three cards that are clearly overpowered. You know that if you acquire them, you’ll probably beat the game. Even worse, sometimes these cards simply don’t appear for many runs. 
- It’s visually dull, with generic sprites for characters and enemies that look like prototypes lacking detail or personality. The color palette also didn’t appeal to me. 
- Animations are very poor. Only a few things move on each screen, and even during big combos or powerful attacks, the animations fail to make the player feel strong. Overall, it looks too static.

Slay the Spire Review: A Full Deck, Half the Obsession
Rating: 7 out of 10

Slay the Spire is what happens when a deck of cards, a dungeon crawler, and a gambling addiction get together and decide sleep is optional. You pick a character, climb a monster filled path/tower, and build your deck one card at a time, attacking enemies, blocking damage, collecting bizarre relics, and making increasingly questionable strategic decisions because surely this card will fix the terrible deck you've accidentally created. Every run reshuffles the enemies, rewards, encounters, and routes, so you're constantly deciding whether to play it safe or risk everything for something shiny. Basically, it's a turn based roguelike where your sword is a deck of cards, your greatest enemy is probability, and “one more run” is the biggest lie you'll tell yourself all night.

* I went into this one knowing its reputation as a genre heavyweight. As someone who enjoys deckbuilders like Balatro and Yu-Gi-Oh!, I was curious whether Slay the Spire would activate those same questionable dopamine receptors.


Pros: "You've Activated My Trap Card!"
+ Cards Do the Heavy Lifting: Attacks, defensive moves, skills, and relics form a straightforward but flexible combat system. Building a deck that complements your character and surviving increasingly difficult encounters is where the game finds its rhythm.
+ A Steady Drip of Dopamine: Choosing new cards after battles keeps each run moving. RNG introduces enough uncertainty that you're constantly weighing immediate survival against building something potentially ridiculous later. One more reward couldn't hurt, right? Famous last words.
+ Easy to Learn, Plenty to Master: The basics click quickly, but understanding synergies, deck efficiency, relic combinations, and enemy patterns introduces considerably more depth. It welcomes newcomers without immediately demanding a PhD in cardboard economics.

Cons: "A Few Cards Short of a Personality"
- The Art Could Use an Upgrade Card: Visuals aren't everything, especially in a card game, but Slay the Spire looks dated. The presentation is functional rather than memorable, and its character and enemy designs rarely command much attention.
- Characters Are More Decks Than Personalities: The playable characters offer different mechanical approaches, but beyond their cards and relic interactions, they don't have much personality to latch onto. They're interesting strategic tools, just not particularly interesting characters.

Neutral: "Draw Two, Manage Expectations"
+/- Familiar Territory: Randomized runs, incremental deckbuilding, risk vs reward decisions, and strategic synergies, it's a recognizable roguelike formula. Slay the Spire executes these systems well, but if you've played plenty of modern deckbuilders, some of its tricks may feel familiar.
+/- The Reputation Is a Double Edged Sword: After years of hearing this described as one of the genre's greats, I expected something that would immediately grab me. I can appreciate the design, understand its influence, and see why players sink hundreds of hours into it. Personally, though, the magic never quite reached those legendary heights.


Verdict
Slay the Spire is a solid deckbuilder with accessible mechanics, meaningful strategic depth, and enough RNG to keep each run interesting. I can understand its reputation and why people have sacrificed entire weekends to the Spire. Unfortunately, after several hours, I was still appreciating the formula more than obsessing over it.

Perhaps the years of hype set my expectations too high, but as someone who loves Balatro and Yu Gi Oh!, I expected a stronger pull. Instead, Slay the Spire mostly reminded me that I should probably revisit those games, which is either a compliment to the genre or a slight failure of customer retention. I don't regret playing it at all, and Slay the Spire 2 has earned a spot on my watchlist. I'm just itching to click the buy button yet.
